issues.issue: "or its successor" is undefined, leaving open which transactions bind a successor Publisher. The phrase could be read to reach asset buyers, mergers, or neither.

The territory is fixed only "approximately" — a radius of "approximately fifty miles" and boundaries "bounded approximately as follows" — so the edge of the Metropolitan Area cannot be located precisely. Whether a given point is inside is genuinely arguable.

Section 22-D directs transfer points 150 miles from Columbus Circle, well outside the fifty-mile Metropolitan Area defined here. The relationship between the defined territory and those distant points is not spelled out.

The recognition clause works from a closed enumeration of occupations, inviting an expressio unius reading that unlisted work is outside the unit. The exception for "Collectors, except in the case of any Publisher using a billing system operated through the auditing department" adds a further boundary question.

Section 2-B extends recognition to "any other operation... even though the same is not expressly hereinabove set forth," which cuts against the closed list here. Which provision controls a newly disputed job is not stated.

"currently performed by a member of the bargaining unit" fixes the condition to an unstated date and to an undefined degree of performance. Whether occasional unit performance satisfies it is arguable.

The catch-all "or other government or municipal building" sits against the enumerated hospital, club comprising one building, and school, leaving its reach open to ejusdem generis argument. The proviso that dealers may fill and collect "according to the current practice in the territory" is likewise unfixed.

The catch-all "any other operation, occupation or branch of work which is now being performed exclusively" is bounded only by an unstated date and by the word "exclusively." Both sides could reasonably dispute what work it sweeps in.
Section 2-A.1's closed list of covered operations pulls the other way, and the two provisions give different answers for work not enumerated. Nothing states which controls.

"new mechanical devices... introduced to perform or aid in the performance of" unit operations is open-ended; "aid in" has no boundary. Whether a device that only partly touches unit work is captured is arguable.

Section 3-D.4-5 contemplates that automated processes and systems may create excess situations and be installed, which sits uneasily with the exclusive-operation guarantee here. The two treat new machinery from opposite directions.
"areas where for any reason distribution is interrupted" places no limit on the Publisher's power to declare an interruption. The trigger for establishing Canada points is effectively unbounded.

The clause forbids substituting buses, ferries or airplanes for "existing means or methods of delivery" and then preserves "the right to make substitution for a bus or railroad now being used," so the prohibition and the saving proviso point opposite ways. Neither "existing means or methods" nor the saved right is defined.

Section 2-E.2(h) lets a Publisher at any time employ railroad, aircraft "or any other form of transportation provided for by this contract," which is hard to square with the restriction here. Their interaction is unaddressed.

Selection is to be "in order of seniority, in accordance with Section 4-B," but 4-B governs the filling of vacant regular situations by qualification and competence, not driver assignment. The cross-reference does not fit the subject.
"A reasonable number of employees" sets no benchmark against which the Publisher's training offering can be measured. The parties could reasonably differ on any given number.

The Publishers' freedom to "select any runs" is hard to reconcile with 2-E.2(e), which requires transfer points "to be agreed upon by the parties" and arbitration if they cannot agree. Unilateral run selection and bilateral transfer-point agreement pull against each other.

Transfer points must be "within the Metropolitan Area but as near the limits of such areas as practical," and "as practical" gives no measurable standard. The location requirement is therefore only loosely fixed.

Section 22-D, Point Two (iii)-(iv), directs The Times to pick transfer points more than 150 miles from Columbus Circle — far outside the fifty-mile Metropolitan Area this paragraph requires. The two cannot both be applied to Times runs on their face.

The requirement that Albany and like runs be driven through to the destination city conflicts with 22-D Point Two, which excepts common-carrier runs over 250 miles and substitutes a transfer point. Which governs a long Times run is not resolved.

The Publisher's right to discontinue runs on a jurisdictional dispute sits against 2-E.2(i)'s promise that no regular situation holder will be laid off as a result of a run. Whether discontinuance may cost situations is unaddressed.

"any other form of transportation provided for by this contract to the extent that such forms of transportation may now be employed" is a general catch-all tied to an unstated baseline. Its reach beyond railroad and aircraft is genuinely uncertain.

Section 2-E.1 bars substituting buses, ferries or airplanes for existing means of delivery absent Joint Standing Committee approval, while this paragraph lets a Publisher employ aircraft "at any time." The consent requirement and the unilateral right conflict.

"laid off solely as a result of the establishment of the run" turns on the word "solely," which is notoriously contestable where a layoff has mixed causes. The provision gives no method for isolating cause.

Section 3-D.1 recognises the Publisher's right to lay off at any time for economic or business reasons, and 3-D.2 says that phrase covers all reasons of an economic character. The no-layoff guarantee here and that broad right must be reconciled.

The exception "present practice, however, excepted" is undefined and undated, and it swallows the tying requirement wherever a contrary practice is asserted. What counts as present practice is not fixed anywhere.

"Conditions and methods of operation now prevailing in the respective mailrooms... shall not be disturbed" identifies neither the conditions nor the date, and "insofar as they affect the jurisdiction of the several unions" adds a second undefined limit. The scope of the freeze is genuinely arguable.

The operative sentence is incomplete — "Any employee shall be entitled to for work" omits the verb (apply), so the right created is not stated. The scope of the right that a defaulting employee then loses depends on that missing word.

"the maximum Union security permissible under the Labor Management Relations Act... to the extent embodied in Section 17" fixes no concrete obligation and defers to a statute and another section. What security is actually required is left to construction.

Section 17-A.1 states that this Agreement eliminates the closed shop because it is no longer permissible, which cuts against the union-security maximum asserted here. The two describe the parties' security arrangement differently.

Section 2-N.3 provides an agency fee for "non-member extras and casuals," contemplating non-members in the unit, while this paragraph requires membership of all regular situation holders. The two coverage rules sit awkwardly together.

The heading is "Work on Sixth Shift" but the operative text speaks of work "in excess of a fifth shift," and the first sentence is ungrammatical ("employed to an the requirements"). Whether the premium attaches to the sixth shift or to any excess work is left unclear.

Section 17-A.1 reprints an italicised "2-L" containing the identical fifth-shift overtime sentence while declaring it "not as a part of this Agreement." The same words are thus both operative here and disclaimed there.

Section 10-B defines a half-day boy as working "in aid of and under the direction of a route man," which is difficult to square with the flat bar here on an employee engaging any person to aid him. The half-day boy exception is not carved out.

The October 26, 1981 letter re Weekly Checkoff permits the Union to convert this monthly deduction schedule to weekly or bi-weekly on sixty days' notice. The amendment mechanism sits outside the section it amends.

Section 22-H sets Times bundle schedules including bundles "weighing 42 pounds or more" and loading rules by weight, and Section 21-D sets News load schedules, which may or may not be constrained by the 46-pound cap here. The relationship between the shop schedules and this general cap is unstated.

"unduly burdensome" is the trigger for the Union's complaint and is given no content, while the Publisher's trigger is the different and equally open phrase "newspaper operational conditions warrant it." Neither standard can be applied from the text.
"unduly burdensome" and "unduly difficult to serve" are the only checks on the Publisher's right and carry no measurable content. What practice crosses the line is left entirely to argument.

Section 16-M.3 forbids any change in condition without the other party's prior consent, whereas this section gives the Publisher a unilateral right to determine wrapping, receipt points and dealers per route. Whether exercising 3-B is a "change in condition" is unresolved.

Section 5-G obliges the Publisher to arrange work weeks "so that as many regular situations as possible may be created and maintained," and 3-D.6 preserves that obligation, while this paragraph recognises an unrestricted right to reduce routes and lay off. The two duties are in tension over the same conduct.

The definition ends in the catch-all "all reasons of an economic or business character," which is circular and expressly refuses any limiting gloss from practice. It gives a court nothing concrete to apply against a contested layoff.

The clause says it does not limit "the Publisher's right to lay off pursuant to Section 3-D" although this paragraph is itself part of Section 3-D, so the reference is self-referential and its intended target (3-D.1) is uncertain. The fifteen-day proviso then qualifies the very right it disclaims limiting.

"conveyor belts, wire-tying machines and the like" is an open catch-all after two specifics, so the reach of "automated process or automated system" is contestable. The clause also protects a list drawn as of May 1, 1981 against automation installed "after May 1, 1965," an unexplained date mismatch.

Section 3-D.1 recognises the Publisher's unqualified right to lay off for economic or business reasons, which the automation no-layoff guarantee here overrides only for listed employees. Where a layoff is both automation-driven and economic the two rules collide.

This savings clause preserves the 5-G obligation to maintain as many regular situations as possible "subject to the terms of Sections 3-D.1 and 16," leaving the layoff right and the maintenance duty each subject to the other. The provision announces the tension without resolving it.

"Methods and extent of direct delivery and combined delivery... as they exist" freezes an undefined and unrecorded baseline. What a "change" to methods and extent is cannot be determined from the words.

Section 3-F lets the Publisher choose and change freely between direct and combined delivery on new sections or routes, the opposite of the freeze here, and the October 26, 1981 "Clarification of Method and Extent" letter reads this section as a subcontracting ban. The boundary between them is unstated.
"new sections or new routes" is the pivot of the provision and is nowhere defined; a rearranged existing route could be called new. The Publisher's freedom turns entirely on that undefined word.

Section 3-E freezes methods and extent of delivery as they exist and forbids change without Joint Standing Committee approval, while this section grants unrestricted freedom for new routes. Whether a route is new or a change to an existing one decides which governs.
"Present practices" is undefined and undated, so the content of what must "continue unaltered" is not ascertainable from the instrument. The good-cause exception is equally open.

Section 12-C repeats this provision word for word, so the same subject is governed by two separately numbered clauses. Duplicate operative text invites argument that one was meant to do different work.

"undue hardship or hazard," "excessive work tasks" and "insofar as practicable" are each standards without content. Whether a given assignment breaches the provision is not determinable from its words.

Coverage is limited to "damages arising out of injuries or death resulting from assaults or other criminal conduct," a general catch-all after one specific, and the amounts "$20,000, $50,000 beginning January 1, 1982" are stated without a connecting word. Both the covered peril and the applicable amount are open to argument.

"shall make every effort" and "in so far as that may be practicable" impose an obligation with no benchmark, and the closing sentences then disclaim any obligation at all. What, if anything, the Publisher must do is genuinely arguable.
"its then fair value" fixes no valuation method or valuer for the Publisher's purchase option. The anti-discrimination proviso is likewise stated without content.

The two sentences overlap: the first commits all advertising and promotional matter to disposal "as the Publisher may direct," while the second requires matter not promoting the Publisher's own publication to be handled by an "extra crew." Which category a given insert falls in, and what an "extra crew" is, cannot be read off the text.

Section 21-D.V(c) declares the "extra crew" requirements of this section inapplicable to commercial work at Newspoint, showing the clause's reach was already contested. The carve-out leaves the residual scope of 3-L undefined.

"best efforts collectively and individually to promote the business and interests of the several Publishers" states a duty with no benchmark and no subject-matter limit. Nothing in the section allows a court to say when it has been breached.

"immediate family shall include" is an inclusive rather than exhaustive formula, so whether relatives outside the long list qualify is open. The proviso that the three days "fall within the regularly scheduled work-week" also leaves partial entitlement unaddressed.

Foremen and assistant foremen are placed on seniority and priority lists here, yet Section 6-B makes the terms of their employment a matter of individual agreement and gives the Publisher an unrestricted right of removal. The two treat supervisory status inconsistently.

"Otherwise seniority is herein defined as length of service based on regularity and continuity of service" gives a second and different meaning of seniority from 4-A.1(a)'s length of service in a regular situation. The word "Otherwise" does not say when each definition applies.

Section 4-B fills vacant regular situations "in accord with their seniority standing," while this paragraph assigns claims to newly created or vacant situations to promotional priority, not seniority. The two allocation rules point to different men.

Group 1 admits men who lost a situation "because of illness, physical incapacity or for other such good and sufficient cause" — a general catch-all after two specifics whose reach is left to the Adjustment Board. Group 3's "men who signify their intention to and do shape steadily" is equally unquantified.

The promotion order lists only Group 1 and Group 3, omitting Groups 2 and 4 that appear in the hiring order, inviting an expressio unius argument that they can never be promoted. Nothing states whether the omission is deliberate.

Section 4-B says vacant situations are filled permanently from among regular situation holders by qualification and seniority, while this subsection is the source of promotion from the extra groups. The interaction of the two routes to a situation is unresolved.
"except where competency is a factor" carves an undefined exception out of the failure-to-shape rule that governs delisting. Whether a man was passed over for competence is not made determinable.

The paragraph makes the Adjustment Board the only body that may add to or change the lists, then allows a foreman to "engage such men as he may be able to obtain" off-list when short-handed. The exclusivity and the foreman's free hand are hard to read together.

The definition of "industry" is syntactically broken — "all companies employing persons engaged in the categories contained in Section 2 hereof by any Publisher, newspaper distributor or wholesaler" — so it is unclear whether the qualifier limits the companies or the persons. A defined term used throughout Section 4 turns on that reading.

The two allocations — one third for non-signatory transfers and two thirds for signatory transfers — are printed as "(4)" and "(34)", so the fractions as written do not correspond to the words. The arithmetic of the annual cap depends on which is right.
"qualified and competent for the work or the job in question" is nowhere defined, and the Agreement provides only that disputes about it go to the Board. The standard itself carries no content.

"the subsequent vacancies not in excess of five created by filling it" and the direction that "the last such subsequent vacancy shall be filled only by a relayman, relief man, bulldog routeman or floorman" leave the sequence of moves genuinely uncertain. The paragraph also says the job is filled "immediately" and then only at the end of a four-week posting.

This section fills vacancies permanently "in accord with their seniority standing," whereas 4-A.1(b) says promotional priority, not seniority, determines who may claim a newly created or vacant regular situation. The two rules select different claimants.

"partial incapacitation by reason of advanced age" and "a leave of absence from the industry" are undefined excusing conditions on which loss of a situation turns. Whether a given absence falls inside them cannot be read off the text.

This paragraph deems the situation vacated automatically after ninety or one hundred twenty days, while subsection (c) makes vacancy depend on a certified letter and a thirty-day explanation period. The "subject to Subsection (c)" tag does not say which date controls.
"shall not be unreasonably withheld" governs both consent and extension without any stated criteria. What refusal is reasonable is left wholly at large.
The situation is preserved "unless an explanation for the absence is received," with no requirement that the explanation be adequate or accepted. Any response would literally defeat the vacancy.

"Employees absent for the foregoing reasons" does not say whether it means only the four excused reasons in 4-F.1(a) or any absence described in that paragraph. Restoration rights turn on that reading.
The weekly maximum is printed as "8915 hours," which is not a possible figure and must stand for thirty-nine and one-half. The written cap on the day work week is therefore not stated in usable form.

"so that as many regular situations as possible may be created and maintained" imposes a duty with no measurable limit — "as possible" is judged against nothing. Whether a given schedule complies is pure argument.

Section 3-D.1 recognises the Publisher's right at any time to reduce routes and lay off for economic reasons, while 3-D.6 expressly preserves the maintenance obligation created here. The right to cut and the duty to maintain govern the same conduct.

This paragraph pays double time for advance-section work on Sunday between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., while 5-K pays time and one-half for Sunday work in exactly the same hours. The two rates cover overlapping work with no priority stated.

Section 16-M.3 forbids any change in condition without the other party's prior consent, whereas this section lets the Publisher change starting times and days off on four days' notice (or pay a premium). Whether a starting-time change needs Union consent is left open.

Section 5-I requires double the regular and overtime rates for advance-section work in the identical Sunday 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. window that this section pays at time and one-half. The instrument does not say which rate applies to that work.

"sufficiently far from where it began to involve substantial travel time" states a threshold with no measure, and the compensation is left to be negotiated later. The provision creates an obligation whose content does not yet exist.

"required or distributed unfairly" is the only limit on the employer's power to compel overtime and carries no stated content. The clause both mandates overtime and makes its imposition challengeable on an undefined ground.

"Present practice regarding the paid lunch period shall prevail as to an outside employee" leaves the entitlement of outside employees wholly undefined and undated. Inside employees get a precise rule and outside employees none.

Foremen's hours and wages are made a matter of private agreement here, yet 4-A.1(a) places foremen on the seniority and priority lists and Section 13 fixes wage scales for the Section 2 operations they may perform. The two schemes overlap without a stated priority.

Only the foreman or assistant-in-charge may "make changes in operating procedures," while 16-M.3 forbids any change in condition without the other party's consent. Whether a foreman's procedural change is a prohibited change in condition is not addressed.

"or days observed as such" is undefined, leaving open when a holiday is treated as falling on another day. The inline definition of an employee who "trips" also turns on the undefined phrase "obtains employment elsewhere in the industry."

The holiday runs from the start of the night shift the night before to the end of the day shift of the holiday, but 5-B defines the night shift as running from 6:00 p.m. to 10:00 a.m., so part of the holiday-night shift falls on the holiday itself. The boundaries of the two definitions do not align.

The premium is written as "price and one-half of the holiday rate," which is not a rate at all and must be read as time and one-half. The sentence as written does not state what the employee is paid after the regular shift.

The bar on rearranging work weeks in a holiday week cannot be squared with 5-J, which lets the Publisher change days off on four days' notice. The exclusion for sick leave also cites "Section 18-B.2," a section that does not exist (sick leave is defined in 13-B.2).

Section 7-C guarantees any employee required to work a holiday "not less than two (2) days' pay for the regular shift worked," while this section pays double the regular and overtime rates when the paper is not issued. Whether the two stack or are the same entitlement is unstated.

The provision fixes where bulk delivery must go but says only that unit employees handle the sections "after such parts or sections reach the platform," leaving who performs the bulk delivery itself unstated. The boundary of union work is therefore drawn by implication only.

Section 9-B addresses the same outside-printed sections but only obliges the Publisher to "endeavor" to have unit employees make the bulk delivery, subject to cost and jurisdiction. The mandatory tone here and the qualified duty there are hard to align.

"shall endeavor" is qualified by the open-ended provisos of "increased cost" and "a jurisdictional conflict with some other union," so the obligation can be defeated by any incremental cost. Whether anything is actually required is genuinely arguable.

The paragraph is both "subject to the provisions herein contained" and open to "such terms as may be agreed upon between such boys and the Publishers." Those two directions cannot both control the half-day boy's terms.

Section 13-C requires that no employee doing work outside Section 2 under a foreman be paid less than the routeman rate, which is difficult to reconcile with freely negotiated half-day boy terms. Nothing states which governs.

A half-day boy is defined as working "in aid of and under the direction of a route man," while 2-M forbids any employee to engage any person to aid him in his assigned work. The two describe the same relationship in incompatible terms.

The cap is set by the number of boys "now employed" and by routes on which none is employed "at this time," with no date fixed for either baseline. In a contract carried forward from earlier agreements, the reference point is genuinely uncertain.

This paragraph permits an increase in the total number of half-day boys on a new route, which is the opposite of the flat cap in 10-G and of the ratchet-down rule in 10-H. The "Except as hereinafter provided" opening is the only bridge.

The ban applies unless the wholesaler is under agreement "or is willing to enter into written collective agreement," a state of mind with no test. "To the extent permitted by law" adds a second undefined qualifier to the whole obligation.

A one-newspaper wholesaler is deemed an employee of the Publisher "subject to all of the terms and conditions hereof, present practices excepted, however" — an undefined exception that can swallow the deeming rule. What "present practices" are excepted is nowhere recorded.

The deemed-employee rule makes such persons subject to the whole Agreement, which sits awkwardly with Section 12-D's separate scheme treating wholesaler employees as covered by a different collective agreement. The two characterisations of the same people differ.
"Present practices" with respect to receipt of newspapers is undefined and undated, so what must continue unaltered cannot be identified from the instrument.

Section 3-G contains the identical sentence, so the same obligation appears twice in separately numbered provisions. Duplicated operative text invites the argument that one of them was meant to do different work.

The Publisher's secondary liability is triggered when the wholesaler fails to pay "within 380 days," a figure that cannot be right and must be thirty. The date on which the Publisher's obligation arises is therefore not stated correctly.
Sub-paragraph (d) applies pension and welfare contributions to "(2), (b), and (c) above," and there is no item (2) — it must mean (a). The scope of the contribution cap depends on that correction.
"the liabilities shall be apportioned by the Publishers so involved" supplies no formula and no mechanism if they disagree. The allocation among Publishers is left entirely open.

"a Publisher who ceases doing business" is undefined, and a merged or suspended newspaper might or might not qualify. Section 18 treats merger, consolidation and permanent suspension as distinct events without linking them to this exclusion.
"reasonable and expeditious arrangements" and "fully and promptly" are the only standards on the Publisher's alternative route to discharging liability. Neither can be applied without argument.

"shall endeavor to have said successor make the payments" creates a duty of effort with no benchmark, in a paragraph otherwise imposing money obligations. Whether the Publisher's efforts sufficed is not determinable.

The $6.00 weekly "allocated to a fringe benefit" is not allocated to any identified benefit, and the conversion to a percentage is only permissive ("may be converted"). What the employer must actually pay in year two is left open.

Sections 13-H.1 and 13-I.1 fix welfare and pension contributions as percentages of the shift rate, and this paragraph contemplates that the $6.00 may instead be contributed to those Funds. How the allocation interacts with the fixed percentages is unstated.

The adjustment is computed by multiplying the excess percentage "by the day scales" and adding the result "to the day scales," leaving the night and Saturday scales unaddressed. Whether and how night rates move is not stated.

Section 19 fixes the Agreement in full force through March 30, 1984, while this paragraph gives the Union a unilateral right to terminate the contract on a wage-control event. The two statements of the term cannot both be absolute.

The last two bands overlap: "more than 223, fewer than 225" gives 19 days and "224 or more" gives 20 days, so an employee with exactly 224 days qualifies under both. The schedule contradicts itself at that figure.

"The vacation schedule shall be arranged at the convenience of the employer, but on the basis of seniority" gives two competing criteria for the same decision. Which yields when they point different ways is not said.

The requirement that "the days of the vacation period shall be consecutive" cannot be squared with 13-B.3, which continues present practices concerning the splitting of vacations. The two govern the same scheduling question oppositely.

The estate receives accrued credits for the previous year "in addition to the maximum vacation pay that he would have received had he worked the full year" of death, a formula that could double-count. "Maximum" is not tied to the 13-B.1 schedule.
"Present practices concerning the splitting of vacations" is undefined and unrecorded, so the content of the continued right is unknown.
Section 13-B.2(a) states flatly that "the days of the vacation period shall be consecutive," which is the opposite of a preserved right to split vacations. The instrument does not say which controls.

This paragraph pays a straight-time day's pay for a holiday falling in a vacation, while 7-C entitles a regular situation holder to a full day's or night's pay for every holiday in his work week. Section 20-D then routes Group 1 holiday pay through both 7-D and this paragraph.

Section 2-K forbids any employee employed in a capacity other than the Section 2 operations from performing those operations, while this paragraph assumes such work is performed under a foreman and only fixes its minimum rate. The two treat non-covered work differently.

"All overtime shall be compensated at a rate of one and a half times the regular hourly rate" cannot be reconciled with 5-H, 5-I and 7-E, which require double the regular and overtime rates for certain Sunday and holiday work. The word "all" leaves no room for those provisions.

The over-scale formula preserves a rate bearing "the same relation to the regular rate fixed herein as their present rate... bears to the regular rate established immediately prior," against a baseline that is nowhere recorded. The sentence as printed is also incomplete.

Section 13-E.2 lets the Publisher modify or abrogate any over-scale arrangement at any time, which would nullify the proportional entitlement created here. The two paragraphs govern the same excess rates in opposite directions.

This paragraph subjects over-scale agreements to the Publisher's control and permits abrogation at any time, while 13-E.1 guarantees the over-scale employee a proportional rate "so long as they continue employed at such operation." The guarantee and the power to abrogate collide.

"each such routeman shall receive two (2) days' pay for such collection" does not say per what period — per collection, per week or per route. The exclusion for Publishers "now billing through the auditing department" is also undated.

"excessive or repeated shortages" is the trigger and has no content, and the relief cap of one-half of one per cent is tied to "the total papers handled" over an unspecified period. Both ends of the provision are open.

Contributions are owed on "each employee's rate per shift for each shift worked by each employee in the bargaining unit," and neither "bargaining unit" nor "rate per shift" is defined for this purpose. Whether casuals, extras and non-members generate contributions, and on what base, is genuinely arguable.

Section 13-H.3 expands "employee" for this Fund to include individuals whose retirement the Trustees recognised, which does not fit a per-shift-worked obligation. The two definitions of the contribution base pull apart.

The definition — "the term 'employee' shall include any individual whose retirement was recognized by the Trustees subsequent to any date on which his employer commenced the payment of contributions in his behalf" — is opaque and sweeps retirees into a term used for active per-shift work. Its boundary cannot be applied as written.

Section 13-H.1 requires contributions only "for each shift worked by each employee in the bargaining unit," a base that cannot accommodate the retirees this paragraph brings within "employee." Read together the contribution obligation becomes indeterminate.

"other employers of individuals working under provisions substantially the same as those of this Agreement" is a general standard with no test of substantial sameness. Which outside employers may contribute is left open.

The contribution base — "8% of each employee's pay rate per shift for each shift worked by each employee in the bargaining unit" — leaves both "employee in the bargaining unit" and "pay rate per shift" undefined, and caps contributions at five shifts "in any payroll week in any one Office." Whether casuals, extras, non-members or shifts worked at another office generate contributions is squarely arguable on these words.

Section 2 defines unit coverage by enumerated operations and 2-B by past exclusive performance, while 13-H.3 expands "employee" for fund purposes; none of these lines up cleanly with "each employee in the bargaining unit" used here. Identifying who generates a pension contribution requires reconciling provisions that were not drafted together.

Eligibility requires "at least six (6) months of priority in the shop as a Group I extra or regular situation holder," mixing the defined terms priority and seniority in a way 4-A.1(b) does not support. How six months of priority is measured is unclear.

Accumulated leave "can be taken at any time during the term of this Agreement" yet must not "interfere with adequate staffing," and "adequate" is given no content. The unqualified right and the staffing limit are stated in the same paragraph without a tie-breaker.
The Publisher's right is to discharge "for cause," a term left undefined and unaccompanied by any list of causes. What suffices is left wholly to construction.

Section 15 gives a remedy to an employee "claiming to have been discharged without just cause," a different and more demanding standard than the "cause" recognised here. The Agreement uses two formulations for the same decision.

"shall make every effort to place such discharged employee at some other operation" sets no benchmark and no consequence for failure. The clause also modifies priority and seniority only "to that extent," which is not quantified.
"a bad driving record" is undefined as a cause of discharge, and "every effort" to place the employee elsewhere carries no measure. Both the trigger and the duty are open.

"otherwise deprived of or injured with respect to any of the rights conferred upon him hereunder" is a general catch-all following the specific instance of discharge. Its reach is not bounded by the text.

This section presupposes a "just cause" standard for discharge, while 14-A recognises the Publisher's right to discharge "for cause" and lets the discharged man be kept out pending determination. The two provisions describe the discharge standard differently.
The waiver rule is disapplied for grievances "found to be continuing grievances," a category the Agreement nowhere defines. Whether a claim is continuing decides whether it is waived entirely.

The impartial member is drawn "from the list compiled in accordance with 16-E. 2. below," yet 16-E.3 speaks of "the existing list of fifteen arbitrators in paragraph 16-E. 1." The Agreement locates the same list in two different paragraphs.

The trigger is that no listed arbitrator is available "within thirty (30) days after his selection," which presupposes a selection that the unavailability is supposed to prevent. The condition is circular as written.
The paragraph refers to arbitrators "listed in Section 16-E. 1," but the list of fifteen is created by 16-E.2. The cross-reference points to the wrong paragraph.

The replacement procedure directs the parties to proceed "by the procedures of 16-E. 2. above" inside 16-E.2 itself, so the provision refers to itself for its own method. Which procedure is meant must be inferred.
The paragraph refers to "the existing list of fifteen arbitrators in paragraph 16-E. 1," but 16-E.1 draws on a list compiled under 16-E.2. The two cross-references cannot both be right.

A quorum of the chairman and two members allows a two-to-one split to decide, while 16-K vests decision power in "a majority of the... Appeals Board" of five. Whether a majority of the quorum or of the full Board is required is unaddressed.

This paragraph speaks of "permanent impartial chairmen designated under Section 16-M," but 16-M.1 provides for a chairman selected annually to serve one contract year at a time. The instrument describes the same office as both permanent and annual.

The Adjustment Board is given "exclusive jurisdiction over any issue arising with regard to the provisions of Section 4-A," yet 4-H sends questions of qualification, competency and the interpretation of the Section 4 provisions to the Joint Standing Committee and/or Appeals Board. Two forums are given the same disputes.

The remedial power "shall include, but shall not be limited to" the enumerated remedies, and extends to safeguarding the rights of "other person." The outer limit of the Board's authority is left open by the catch-all.

The October 26, 1981 letter provides that the present status quo arbitrator and alternate "shall continue to serve in their present respective capacities" until replacements are selected, cutting across the fixed annual terms set here. The two provisions fix the chairman's tenure differently.

"change in condition" is the operative term and is nowhere defined, so the reach of the consent requirement is entirely open. The exception is also written as a layoff "as hereinbefore provided in Section 8-D," a section that does not exist (layoff is Section 3-D).

The consent requirement cannot be squared with the express unilateral rights elsewhere — 3-B (manner of wrap, routes and dealers), 3-D.1 (rearranging routes and deliveries) and 5-J (changing starting times and days off on four days' notice). Each of those lets a Publisher act without the Union's consent.

Only "the Union" may ask the chairman to order restoration, although 16-M.3 makes the no-change rule binding on "either party." The remedy is written one-sidedly against the party that drafted the rule as mutual.

This paragraph makes the Impartial Chairman the fifth member for change-of-condition grievances, while 16-E.1 requires the fifth member to be drawn at random from the arbitrator list for every matter referred to the Appeals Board. The two selection rules can both claim the same case.

The no-strike promise is subject to an exception "as against the party failing to comply with a decision, award or order," which permits self-help on a contested question of compliance. Who decides non-compliance before the exception is invoked is not said.

Section 11-B contemplates that "the failure to comply" may itself be controverted and must go to the Joint Standing Committee or Appeals Board, which is hard to square with an immediate right to strike on the same ground. The two treat non-compliance differently.

This recital declares the italicised material "printed below... for reference only and not as a part of this Agreement," while 17-A.2 provides that the same italicised provision "automatically shall become a part of this Agreement" if the legal bar lifts. The instrument both excludes and conditionally includes the same text.

The reproduced provision is textually incomplete — "such men to be comtion for which they are required" omits an entire clause — so what the furnished men must be is unstated. Its terms would nonetheless become operative under 17-A.2.

The second sentence of this italicised text is identical to the operative fifth-shift overtime rule in 2-L.3, yet 17-A.1 says the italicised material is not part of the Agreement. The same words are both operative and disclaimed.

The trigger is that a provision "no longer is held to be inoperative" by legislative enactment or by decision of "the court of highest resource," a garbled phrase, and the revival is limited to what is "permitted." When and to what extent the italicised text springs back is genuinely uncertain.

Section 17-A.1 states that the italicised provision is "not as a part of this Agreement," which this paragraph contradicts by making it automatically part of the Agreement on a contingency. The two paragraphs of the same section point opposite ways.

"the spirit as well as the letter of this Agreement is to be observed in full" invites obligations beyond the written terms without identifying any. What the spirit requires is by definition not on the page.

The parties declare they have bargained and "settled the same for the term of this Agreement," yet 20-B (joint study of clerical work), 21-G.2 (zone routes to be negotiated) and the 1981 side letters on pension and Lancaster commit them to further negotiation during the term. The closure asserted here is contradicted by those provisions.

Section 12-D.1.3(e) caps a Publisher's liability for suspension and merger pay at 15 days for a wholesaler's employees, while this section gives covered regular situation holders the cash equivalent of eight weeks. The Agreement fixes two very different measures of the same benefit.

This section directs that the contract be treated "as an individual agreement" between the Union and each Publisher, although the opening Agreement is made by the Publishers' Association as agent for both and Sections 16 and 18 operate through Association-designated bodies and industry-wide funds. Whether the instrument is one multiemployer contract or two is left unresolved.
The mediation deadline is printed as "thirty (36) days," so the figure and the words disagree. Which controls the timetable is not stated.

This subsection explains the seventy-five day notice by reference to a sixty-five day period that appears nowhere else in the Agreement. The recital of purpose does not match the operative notice provision in 19(a).

The first sentence pays unused leave days "at his normal straight-time weekly pay" and the second pays the balance "at the rate he receives for the majority of his shifts," two different rates for what appears to be the same payment. The paragraph does not say when each applies.
Section 13-K.2 provides that unused leave is liquidated and paid "at the prevailing rate," a third formulation of the same entitlement. The three rate provisions cannot all be applied.

The paragraph promises only a joint study "to define the types of clerical work which are appropriate to the deliverer's bargaining unit," creating no rule and no consequence if the study fails. Whether any clerical work is presently in the unit is left undecided.

"overtime which would normally be assigned to employees who are paid a higher rate" turns on the undefined word "normally" and on a comparison with no baseline. Whether a given assignment is barred cannot be read off the text.

Holiday pay is directed "in accordance with Section 13-B. 4," which pays a straight-time day for a holiday in a vacation, while eligibility is tested under 7-D, which concerns extras' holiday pay; and the proviso gives the Foreman discretion over vacation scheduling although 13-B.2(a) requires scheduling on the basis of seniority. The cross-references do not fit together.

The memorandum opens "Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary in the Agreement," which displaces unidentified provisions of Sections 3, 4 and 5 for bulldog phase-outs. Which provisions yield is left to be worked out.

Vacant and newly created situations must go to "excess situation holders" here, while 4-B and 4-A.2(c) allocate the same vacancies by posting, seniority and promotion from Groups 1 and 3. The two filling rules compete for the same jobs.

The sentence runs together a waiver of layoff rights, an exception for excess situation holders "seventy (70) or more years of age," and a clause that "nor shall the provisions of Sections 3 and 4 of the Agreement be applicable to them" — with "them" capable of meaning either group. Which employees lose the protection of Sections 3 and 4 is genuinely unclear.

Disapplying Sections 3 and 4 removes the layoff, seniority and recall machinery of 3-D.1, 4-E and 4-A for the affected men. That cannot be reconciled with 20-E.3's promise that no such situation holder will be laid off.

Starting times and days off of excess situation holders are placed "at the discretion of the Publishers," while 5-J requires four days' notice (or a premium) for such changes and 16-M.3 requires consent to a change in condition. The three rules govern the same act differently.
"The Times will continue its present practice" leaves The Times' paycheck-correction obligation wholly undefined while The News is given a 48-hour rule. What the present practice is appears nowhere.

The provision applies to questions "which are subject to arbitration under the contract and which are submitted to arbitration," then says they will be arbitrated under Section 16 — a circular statement that adds nothing. Whether it makes any Sunday-section change arbitrable is unclear.

The obligation is keyed to sections "currently known as Section 2 (Living) and Section 3 (Leisure)" and to printing "on its own present press equipment," all fixed to an unstated date. Renaming or re-equipping would put the clause's application in doubt.

The limitation is framed by reference to nine months ending June 30, 1974 and succeeding quarters through March 1975, periods long past when this 1981-84 Agreement took effect. The closing Memorandum that every side agreement "shall be continued through the term of this agreement and deemed updated" gives no way to update these dates.

This provision says the all-advertising-section agreement "ends effective March 30, 1975," yet it is reproduced as an operative shop condition of a contract running from March 31, 1981 to March 30, 1984, and the closing Memorandum continues every memorandum "through the term of this agreement and deemed updated." Whether 21-B has any force during this term cannot be determined.

The overtime entitlement is triggered "when the regular roto is 75, 60, 50, 40 or fewer copies per load," an enumeration whose relationship to the trailing "or fewer" is unclear, and it is granted to four named individuals only. Whether the benefit survives those men is not addressed.

The 240-load ceiling for News trucks sits alongside the Newspoint schedules in 21-D, which permit up to 300 loads, and the general load schedules under 3-A.2. Which limit governs a given News truck is not stated.

"no reduction in the present number of a.m. routes as a result of home delivery" turns on a causal test with no method of proof, and "present" is fixed only by the recital that "there are now 133 a.m. routes." Both the baseline and the causation requirement are open.

Section 3-D.1 gives each Publisher the right from time to time to reduce and rearrange routes as it finds necessary or desirable, which this guarantee restricts for a.m. routes. The two provisions govern the same decision.

The second sentence promises only that the Union will "send letter that it will meet to resolve a problem of overtime... if, under normal operation, one arises," which creates no ascertainable obligation. "Normal operation" is undefined.

This paragraph requires tailmen above 180 loads "except as provided in the Newspoint Agreement," while the 21-D schedules set entirely different load thresholds for tailmen (up to 300 loads under Schedule A). The exception does not say which schedule prevails outside Newspoint.
"Bindery Operation — Transport men hired according to need" states no standard, no decision-maker and no number. Whose judgment of "need" governs is entirely unstated.

The column is headed maximum loads "with o Tailmen" yet the closing sentence says tailmen will be employed on all runs under Schedule A except recovery runs, so it is unclear whether the figures are with or without a tailman. The papers-per-load column also runs 150, 100, 45, 50, 40, which is out of sequence.
The column heading carries an asterisk whose footnote does not appear with this schedule, so the consequence of exceeding the Suffolk figures is not stated here. The table is incomplete on its face.

The footnote "If these schedules are exceeded then Schedule 'A' will apply" does not say whether Schedule A's load limits or its tailman requirement is what follows. The consequence of exceeding the franchise figures is ambiguous.

"Present practice with respect to running time" is undefined and unrecorded, so the running-time entitlement cannot be determined from the instrument. Section 22-D(ix) fixes run time by a mileage rule for The Times but nothing does so here.

"present practice will be continued" leaves the pallet-truck loading limit entirely undefined, in contrast with the precise 250-load figure in the preceding paragraph. What practice is preserved appears nowhere.

The manning schedule applies only to "Day side, double out only" and provides "8 general floormen to be used when and where needed as directed," leaving other operating conditions unmanned by the text. What governs when the plant is not double out is unstated.

A worked lunch or coffee break is to be "compensated as provided in Section 5N," but 5-N compensates only a worked paid lunch at one-half hour at time and one-half and says nothing about coffee breaks or a forty-five minute period. The cross-reference does not supply a rate for what this paragraph creates.

The obligation turns on the "contractually designated 'territorial coverage' of the Union," which Section 1 fixes only "approximately" by a fifty-mile radius and approximate boundary towns. Whether a delivery point is inside cannot be settled without construing Section 1.

Delivery is to "points designated by The News," with the only limit that their location "will be in line with current policy" — an undefined and unrecorded standard. The Publisher's discretion is effectively unbounded.

This sub-paragraph disapplies the "extra crew" requirements of Section 3-L to commercial work at Newspoint, leaving 3-L's reach elsewhere to be worked out. The carve-out identifies a contested boundary without fixing it.

The paragraph guarantees that the 58 named day-side men "will continue to be employed on the day side" and then denies that it is "a guaranty of 58 day jobs," while also preserving the Union's right to argue that vacated jobs stay on the day side. The commitment and its disclaimer largely cancel each other.

This paragraph supersedes "all other agreements, memoranda or practices" applicable to Newspoint, while the closing Memorandum provides that "every memorandum, letter agreement or side agreement shall be continued through the term of this agreement and deemed updated." The two clauses give opposite answers for Newspoint side agreements.

"The IBM stipulation" is referred to without being identified, reproduced or dated, so the content of what continues is unknowable from the instrument. Its limitation to "the Daily News only" cannot cure that.

This sentence repeats the substance of 21-C.3(e) ("Home delivery runs will not service any dealers other than franchise dealers") in different words. Two formulations of the same restriction invite argument that they differ.
"reviewed and revised in a fair and equitable manner" states no criterion, no timetable and no decision-maker for the locker arrangement. Nothing in it can be applied without supplying a standard.

One week's notice of a change in method of delivery on a holiday night is hard to square with 16-M.3, which forbids any change in condition without the other party's prior consent, and with 5-J's four-day rule. Three different notice or consent regimes can cover the same change.

The actuaries are to determine the funding cost "for the calendar year 1966" and the options in paragraph 2 turn on March 31, 1970 dates, all long past when this 1981-84 Agreement took effect. The closing Memorandum deeming side agreements "updated" gives no way to update those years.

The Union "shall select one option" with no deadline and no default if it does not, so the Publisher's obligation may never crystallise. The option itself is fixed to retirements "on or after March 31, 1970."

Benefits for service after March 31, 1970 are to be provided "under a new pension plan, the terms of which shall be jointly agreed upon" — an agreement to agree with no fallback. If the parties do not agree the option is empty.

The trigger sentence is ungrammatical and conditions everything on what "is mutually agreed," and the benefit is only "comparable improvements" judged by whether another agreement is "taken in their entirety" more favorable. Neither the trigger nor the measure of the obligation can be applied as written.

The October 7, 1981 letter separately promises the Union whatever pension, welfare and insurance increases the Publishers grant any other labor organization, subject to different provisos. Two most-favored-nation promises of different scope cover the same subject.

This is a recital of what the parties "acknowledged" and "recognize" about efficiency and impact, and it points toward The News's operating needs while the operative 21-G.2 gives the Union an absolute veto. The recital and the operative term pull in different directions.

"such a concept" is identified only as the "zone" route concept "used at Newspoint as it might be introduced into the black and white operation," which does not fix what is being vetoed. How far a change must go before it is the concept is arguable.

The absolute requirement of NMDU agreement cannot easily be squared with 3-B and 3-D.1, which give the Publisher the right to determine routes and to rearrange deliveries as it finds desirable. The boundary between a zone concept and ordinary route rearrangement is unaddressed.

The provision breaks off mid-sentence — "will expire in three years [from March 31," — so the expiry date is not stated in the text. A separately expiring shop agreement inside a fixed-term contract needs that date.

The parties "commit themselves to the achievement of maximum productivity and efficiency" while the same paragraph preserves the Union's right to negotiate manning "to avoid undue hardships." Both are standards without content and they point in opposite directions.

These recital-style minutes commit to maximum productivity "consistent with the terms of this memorandum and of the contract," while the operative Carlstadt jurisdiction provisions that follow allocate exclusive work regardless of efficiency. The introductory commitment and the operative jurisdiction terms are in tension.

The paragraph runs two subjects together — offloading jurisdiction and the placing of colour sections before mailroom operations — and the sentence beginning "In addition" is broken by intruding text about the Sta-Hi Newstrack. What is actually agreed about colour-section placement cannot be read off the page.

The definition of an insert tying line is word-for-word identical to the definition of a press tying line later in the same Minutes. Two distinct terms given the same definition cannot be told apart for jurisdictional purposes.

Jurisdiction extends to ITLs destined for city delivery "or percentage equivalent of the city circulation which is approximately 4," a figure that is not a percentage and cannot be applied. The share of the work allocated is therefore unstated.

This definition of a press tying line is identical, word for word, to the definition of an insert tying line earlier in the same Minutes. The two defined terms carry different jurisdictional consequences but cannot be distinguished on these words.

Jurisdiction over PTLs is fixed by newspapers "destined for New York City or percentage equivalent of city circulation," without stating what that percentage is or how it is calculated. The alternative measure is left blank.

The paragraph as printed has no subject — it begins "truck loaders, including, but not limited to, operations, control and clearing of jams" — so the grant of jurisdiction over the Sta-Hi Newstrack is incomplete. The "including but not limited to" catch-all then leaves the covered tasks open.

Console jurisdiction extends to "any other operation under the jurisdiction of the delivery department," a catch-all that makes the section's own list of ITLs, PTLs, Newstrack and truck loaders redundant. Its reach depends on jurisdiction determined elsewhere.

The general statement sweeps in "any operations over which the delivery department had jurisdiction at 43d Street, whether by contract or by precedent," a catch-all sitting against the carefully enumerated operations in the same Minutes. Jurisdiction "by precedent" is not recorded anywhere and its boundary is unfixed.

The enumeration of specific Carlstadt operations invites an expressio unius reading that unlisted work is excluded, which this clause reverses. Whether the specific allocations or this residual clause governs a new dispute is unstated.

The break entitlement is written as "either two 165-minute coffee breaks or one 80-minute coffee break," figures that are internally inconsistent and cannot both be alternatives. The actual break length is not stated correctly.

Truck loaders are given "80 minutes for lunch" while floormen in the preceding paragraph get forty, a figure that is almost certainly a mistake for thirty and reverses the evident hierarchy. The lunch entitlement as written does not match the scheme.

The relief periods stated here — 20 minutes per trailer and 15 minutes per suburban or mail bag truck — are separately granted by 22-C(d), with disputes there referred to Theodore Kheel rather than Section 16. The same entitlement appears twice under different dispute machinery.

The obligation is keyed to runs handled "as of November 1, 1975" and to conversion within sixty days of ratification, dates belonging to an earlier agreement carried into this 1981-84 contract. Whether it has any operation during this term is not resolved by the closing Memorandum deeming side agreements updated.

The deadline "No later than March 31, 1977" had passed years before this Agreement took effect on March 31, 1981, and the 150-mile transfer point it authorises lies far outside the Metropolitan Area required by 2-E.2(e). The provision cannot be applied on its own terms in this term.

The sentence breaks off — "provided that such other destination is at a location further" — so the condition on alternative destinations is unstated. The permitted destinations cannot be identified from the text.

This paragraph eliminates the Hightstown transfer point, yet 22-D Point Two (iv) lists Hightstown, New Jersey among the transfer points in use that fix the minimum distance for future selections. One provision abolishes what the other treats as a benchmark.

The obligation is measured by papers delivered "as of November 1, 1975" and by a sixty-day period after ratification, dates carried over from a prior agreement. Whether anything remains to be done during this term is unclear.

This paragraph operates by amending "Paragraph (ix) on Page 85 of the 1973-75 contract booklet," a superseded document, whereas the current text of 22-D Point Two (ix) already reads 27 miles. The amendment has nothing left to act on in this Agreement.

The Philadelphia run time is fixed at nine hours, while 22-D Point Two (ix) sets run time by the rule of one hour for every 27 miles from The Times to a single destination. The two methods give different answers for the same run.

"Combos and 5/3 sheets will be 'kicked off' in variables of five" uses undefined shop jargon, and the Sunday completes are to continue "as heretofore," an unrecorded practice. Neither half of the sentence can be applied from the instrument.
The parties will only "observe the new conveyor system to determine manpower requirements," which creates no manning obligation and no method of resolution. What follows the observation is unstated.

A manning change following installation would be a "change in condition" requiring the other party's consent under 16-M.3, which this open-ended observation clause does not address. The two provisions govern the same eventuality.

Relief disputes are sent to a named individual, Theodore Kheel, while Section 16-A requires all disputes over interpretation or application of the Agreement to go to the Joint Standing Committee and Appeals Board under the arbitrator-selection machinery of 16-E. Two incompatible forums are provided.

The decisions "relate to the future; they are prospective" and 2-E.2 continues to apply "until they are in force," but nothing states when or how they come into force. Whether the modifications operate at all during this term is left open.

Section 2-E.2 as written continues to govern existing runs while this memorandum modifies it prospectively, so the same runs may be governed by either text depending on an unstated trigger. The relationship between the two is not resolved.

Section 2-E.2 is said to apply "fully, except as to such modifications as are described in this letter," yet those modifications directly displace the transfer-point rule in 2-E.2(e). The instrument thus contains two inconsistent versions of paragraph (e) for The Times.

"The Times will begin to apply the principle" sets no timetable and no measure of compliance, and the exception for runs "more than 250 miles from Columbus Circle or which have more than two stops" can be reshaped by adding a stop. The obligation is only aspirational as written.

This defines a transfer point and lets The Times select its location subject to Union agreement, whereas 2-E.2(e) requires transfer points to be "within the Metropolitan Area but as near the limits of such areas as practical" with disputes to the Impartial Chairman. The location rule and the dispute route both differ.

Transfer points for long runs must be "more than 150 miles from Columbus Circle," while 2-E.2(e) requires them to be inside the Metropolitan Area, which Section 1 defines as a radius of approximately fifty miles. The two location rules cannot both be satisfied.

The floor is "any transfer point in use as of the date of signing of this Agreement," but this memorandum was negotiated for the 1970 contract and reproduced in the 1981-84 book, so the operative date is uncertain. The named points also include Hightstown, which 22-A abolishes.
The 150-mile ceiling and the named benchmark points lie outside the Metropolitan Area within which 2-E.2(e) requires transfer points to be located. The two provisions fix incompatible geography.

Drivers who work 45 hours without a fifth shift receive benefit credits "as if they worked the fifth shift (vacation, sick days, pension and welfare, etc.)," while 13-H.1 and 13-I.1 tie welfare and pension contributions to shifts actually worked, capped at five. The instrument creates a credit for a shift that generates no contribution.

The Times must "promptly use every practical legal means to implement the new runs" and, if legal action cannot resolve the problem, the change is abandoned — a standard with no content and an escape with no test. Who determines that legal action cannot resolve the problem is unstated.

The obligations are keyed to January 1, 1974 and to runs "presently delivered" to United and Farer, dates and facts from a prior agreement carried into this 1981-84 contract. The closing Memorandum deeming side agreements updated supplies no new dates.

The parties agree only "to meet promptly... to discuss the feasibility" of direct suburban delivery, which imposes no substantive obligation. The list "such as Boston, Washington, Baltimore, etc." is also open-ended.

The mileage rule applies to a run "direct from The Times to a single destination," and for multi-destination runs the text says only that "allowance will be made" without any measure. Run time for the common multi-stop case is left undetermined.

The opening words are broken — "Paragraph (h) will be construed clude this stipulation" — and the seasonal-factor exception is explained only by a single example. Whether a given assignment is seasonal cannot be determined from the text.

Section 2-E.2(h) lets a Publisher "at any time" increase, decrease or discontinue over-the-road trucking, while this stipulation forbids The Times from assigning a nine-month-old run to a common carrier. The unrestricted right and the restriction cover the same conduct.

This memorandum was "negotiated in connection with the agreement effective March 31, 1970," yet its references to "the term of this Agreement" are reproduced in the 1981-84 book. Which term the named situations are protected for is unresolved.

"As of the last day of this Agreement" is ambiguous in a memorandum negotiated for the 1970 contract but printed in the 1981-84 book and continued by the closing Memorandum. Whether these situations already converted to floor situations years ago cannot be told.

The new schedule is described only as showing "the following changes from the schedule now in use," a baseline that is undated and not reproduced. What the resulting schedule is cannot be derived from the text alone.

Section 3-A.1 requires each Publisher to continue in effect "the schedules shown in the last notice of such schedules to the Union," subject to the 46-pound cap, while this section directs a new schedule. Which schedule governs, and whether the change needed 3-A.4 arbitration, is unaddressed.

The loading rule reads "bundle weight of 87 to 46 pounds, five high," a range that runs backwards and exceeds the 46-pound maximum, and the Saturday exception is limited only by "a reasonable number of bundles." Neither the range nor the exception can be applied as written.

The parties are to meet to review the schedule, the Union's ability to pay "and other relevant factors," with no consequence attached to that review. Whether the payment schedule can be altered as a result is not said.

"more favorable terms or treatment with respect to the payment or disposition called for by an arbitration award or judicial decree" gives no way to compare across differently structured settlements. Whether another union's treatment is more favorable is a matter of judgment the clause does not guide.

Acceleration is triggered if the Union violates "the provisions against strikes and disruptions of orderly relationships," but no such provision against "disruptions of orderly relationships" is identified anywhere. The condition of default cannot be located.

Section 16-N contains the only no-strike undertaking, and it expressly permits a strike against a party failing to comply with a Board decision. That exception is irreconcilable with an unqualified acceleration on any strike.

Notice is required before "any major change in its operations which has an impact on a significant number of its NMDU employees," and neither "major" nor "significant number" is defined; the single example does not fix the boundary. When notice is owed is left to argument.

Section 16-M.3 requires the other party's prior consent before any change in condition, while this memorandum requires only thirty days' notice for a major operational change. Notice and consent are different obligations for what may be the same act.

The memorandum incorporates "the three points concerning changed conditions contained in the 1971 decision of Arbitrator Peter Seitz" without stating them, so its content is unknowable from the instrument. It also depends on an oral opinion in another arbitration.

The memorandum contemplates that the meaning of Section 16-M will be supplied by an arbitrator's written decision rather than by the text, while 16-M.3 states the no-change rule and 16-M.5 fixes the forum. The Agreement thus leaves its own change-of-conditions rule to be written elsewhere.

"Every memorandum, letter agreement or side agreement shall be continued through the term of this agreement and deemed updated" identifies no documents and gives no method of updating. What "deemed updated" does to obsolete dates and figures cannot be worked out from the words.

This blanket continuation cannot be squared with 21-B.4 (that agreement "ends effective March 30, 1975"), 21-G.3 (expiry in three years) or 21-D.VIII (which supersedes all other Newspoint memoranda). Several side agreements are simultaneously continued and terminated.

The Supplementary Agreement declares itself "within the terms of the current collective bargaining agreement" while item 4 guarantees starting times that 5-J allows the Publisher to change. Whether it supplements or overrides the main text is unstated.

The foreman may assign the utility man to jobs "including but not limited to" three examples, yet the last sentence makes clearing "log jams in the machine room" work only the utility man may do. The open assignment power and the exclusive reservation sit oddly together, and "log jams" does not match the earlier "clearing jams."

The paragraph guarantees at least eighty-one combined floor hires and then provides for what happens "should the number of men hired be reduced as herein set forth," although nothing in it sets forth any reduction. The reduction mechanism it presupposes is missing.

This guarantees regular situation holders against any change in starting times, while 5-J expressly permits the Publisher to change a situation holder's reporting time on four days' notice. The guarantee and the notice provision cannot both apply to the same men.

The route "shall be filed by in-shop bidding" — "filed" for "filled" — and "in-shop bidding" is not the posting and bidding procedure described anywhere in Section 4. How the route is to be awarded is not clearly stated.

The letter commits to a past practice of posting job descriptions "including, but not limited to" three items and then says the practices "do not limit either party's rights under the collective bargaining agreement." The undertaking is largely cancelled by its own reservation.

The parity promise is defeated where improvements are given "in exchange for productivity improvements (as determined to the Union's reasonable satisfaction) or are diverted from the negotiated pattern package" — two undefined and untested carve-outs. Whether the promise ever bites depends on them.

Section 21-F.3 contains a differently worded most-favored-nation promise by The News for pension improvements, judged by whether another agreement is "taken in their entirety" more favorable. Two overlapping parity clauses with different tests cover the same benefits.

The status quo arbitrator is to continue indefinitely until a replacement assumes office, whereas 16-M.1 fixes annual terms and 16-G provides that the term of the permanent impartial chairmen ends with the Agreement. The tenure rules do not match.

The letter refers to "the list of arbitrators provided by Section 16-E.1," but the list of fifteen is compiled under 16-E.2 and is subject to the annual striking procedure of 16-E.3. The holdover promised here cuts across that procedure.

The letter empowers the Union unilaterally to amend Section 2-N.1's monthly deduction timetable on sixty days' notice, an amendment mechanism found nowhere in the Agreement itself. Which text governs deduction timing until notice is given is left implicit.
The letter says only that "The Times is happy to continue our discussions and review of this subject," which creates no obligation of any kind. Whether it is a contractual term at all is arguable.

Section 17-D records that the parties have bargained and "settled the same for the term of this Agreement," while this letter keeps pension proposals open for discussion during the term. The closure clause and the open item point different ways.

The Times agrees only "to discussion concerning the feasibility of this proposal before the operation begins," with the underlying transport proposal conditioned on "increased costs" that are not defined. Nothing enforceable is fixed.

This letter states flatly that The News and the Union "will establish a Payroll Deduction Savings Program," while the same letter's later paragraph makes the programme conditional on "a sufficient number of employees" being interested. The commitment is both unconditional and conditional.

The programme depends on "a sufficient number of employees" being interested and on "another acceptable bank," neither of which is defined or committed to any decision-maker. Whether the obligation is ever triggered cannot be determined.

Safety bars are required on "all trucks used for over-the-road runs (Long Island routes, news company runs, all other long runs)," where the catch-all "all other long runs" has no defined boundary. Which vehicles must be equipped therefore turns on an undefined term.

The letter promises that after six payments The News "will not, under any circumstances, require additional payments," while paragraph 3 of the accompanying Memorandum of Understanding accelerates the entire remaining balance if the Union strikes. The absolute release and the acceleration clause collide.

The commitment is to abide by "the arbitration award concerning the 48 inch height from the top of the skid," an award neither identified by date or parties nor reproduced. Its content is not ascertainable from the instrument.
The sentence is incomplete — "Furthermore, The News will abide by all" — so the class of Newspoint agreements it undertakes to observe is unstated. The obligation has no object as written.

Even completed as a promise to abide by all Newspoint written agreements, it sits against 21-D.VIII, which supersedes and replaces all other agreements, memoranda or practices applicable to Newspoint. One preserves what the other displaces.

A memorandum expressly deleted from the Agreement is revived if "there should be a problem in the future arising thereunder," with no definition of a problem and no reference to the memorandum's terms. A deleted document is thus made conditionally operative on an untestable trigger.

Eligibility for "the Medill Plan" is committed to rules the Benefit Department will post, so the eligibility terms are set unilaterally and are not in the instrument. The plan itself is not identified elsewhere in the Agreement.

The deduction runs for "a reasonable period of time designated by the employee" and requires an assignment "satisfactory to the Publisher," giving each side an undefined discretion. Whether a given assignment must be honoured is left open.

The acknowledgement that the Agreement "prohibits the subcontracting of bargaining unit deliveries except as it may exist pursuant to the contract" is circular: the exception is defined by the very contract said to contain the prohibition. Neither the prohibition nor its exception can be located in the words.

No provision of the Agreement states a subcontracting prohibition, and Sections 3-E, 3-F and 12-A expressly contemplate delivery through wholesalers and news companies. This letter characterises the contract in terms its operative provisions do not bear out.

The obligation arises only "when the planned DEC System is installed and operational," an event with no date and within The News's own control. Whether the promise is ever triggered is not determinable.
The annual pension statement is again conditioned on the planned DEC System being "installed and operational," an undated contingency in the employer's hands. The duty may never mature.

This letter contemplates "credited shifts for which contributions were not made," whereas 13-I.1 ties contributions to each shift worked in the bargaining unit subject to a five-shift weekly cap. The instrument does not explain how a shift can be credited without a contribution.
The thirty-day deadline yields "if delayed because of an emergency or Act of God," where "emergency" is an undefined general term sitting beside the specific Act of God. Its reach is left open.

The item records only that the Union "requested" side-door vans and "was advised that such vans would be ordered," which reads as a minute of discussion rather than a promise. Whether it creates any obligation is arguable.

The letter is dated November 3, 1978 and refers to "the present Collective Bargaining Committee," yet it is printed in the 1981-84 book and carried forward by the Memorandum continuing every side agreement "deemed updated." What survives of a three-year-old minute is unclear.
The Company only "would explore the purchase and use of dehumidifiers," which imposes no duty to purchase, install or report. Nothing here can be enforced.
The paragraph records only that "the Company indicated that new trucks had been ordered," a statement of fact rather than an undertaking. Whether it binds anyone to anything is genuinely doubtful.

"Sixers" is undefined shop jargon and the entitlement is fixed only "in the same percentage as they are currently available to the Newspoint day shift," an unrecorded baseline. Neither the thing promised nor its quantity can be identified.
The Company agreed that five named jobs "would be defined when posted," without saying what the definitions must contain or who settles them. The promise has no ascertainable content.
"The Union agreed to meet and discuss the printing of commercial sheets" fixes no time, no subject-matter limit and no outcome. It is an agreement to talk only.

The manning at 43rd Street will only be "reviewed within a reasonable time... but in no event later than sixty (60) days," with no obligation to change anything and no standard for the review. The provision produces no determinable result.
